body: Street View coverage in Laos is very limited to five cities: Vientiane, Vang Vieng, Luang Prabang, Savannakhet, and Pakse. All coverage was taken by a Generation 3 camera. Each city has a distinct look, making them easily distinguishable.

In all cities except for the capital, Vientiane, a silver-coloured Google car with a roof rack and two metal bars is visible. A similar car can be found in Guatemala, so be sure to look at the other clues before guessing.
Laos drives on the right-hand side of the road. This is a key differentiator from neighboring Thailand, which drives on the left.

Laotian licence plates are typically short and yellow, which helps distinguish them from the white plates used in Thailand and Cambodia for non-commercial vehicles. Commercial plates in Laos are white, and government plates are blue.
Lao script is compact and curvy, with some diacritics on top and below characters. It is very similar to Thai script, but Lao script generally has fewer straight lines.

Laos is a majority Buddhist country, so Buddhist temples with ornate, often gold-leafed, decorations are a common sight. However, it's important to remember that Thailand and Cambodia are also majority Buddhist.
Striped curbs of various colors like red, yellow, or black and white can be seen throughout Laos.

Stop signs in Laos feature Lao script, sometimes with the word 'stop' in Latin script below. A key distinguishing feature is that Laotian stop signs have only 2 characters, while those in Thailand have 3.
Laos uses distinctive square concrete poles with a row of small pinholes down the sides. Similar poles can be found in Thailand, Sri Lanka, and sometimes Cambodia.
Laos uses square, concrete black and white bollards with one or more black bands. Similar bollards are also used in Thailand, Indonesia, and occasionally Cambodia.
Some lamp posts in Laos have diagonal red and white striped markings that do not extend all the way down to the base.
A red and white painted cuboid concrete bollard can sometimes be seen a few meters off the side of the road.
Laos has a communist government, so you may occasionally see red hammer and sickle flags.
Luang Prabang is situated on the Mekong River and is surrounded by low mountains and hills.
Palm trees are a common sight in Luang Prabang.

Luang Prabang, a UNESCO heritage site and former royal capital, features a wealth of historical architecture, including numerous temples and buildings with traditional dark wooden elements. Some structures also date back to the period of French colonial rule.
Within Laos, blue sign backs are exclusively found in Luang Prabang.

The most reliable way to recognize Vang Vieng is by its distinctive rugged mountain range, which is visible from most locations. However, be aware that Street View coverage in Vang Vieng is extremely limited.
Vang Vieng is a highly touristic town, with numerous signs for hotels, guesthouses, and other tourist-oriented businesses.

The Vientiane area is unique in Laos as the Google car is not visible, and it includes significant rural coverage. This can create confusion with Thailand and Cambodia, so it's important to use other clues like the driving side to differentiate them.
Road 450, located east of Vientiane, is constructed entirely of concrete blocks and is one of the few divided highways in Laos with Street View coverage.
The divided highway passing through Nong Beuak is easily identified by the unique street lamps that line the road.

The road through the conservation area is characterized by its uniquely hilly terrain for Laos, a dry, forested landscape, and good condition with colored curbs. It is the only single-lane road with black and white or yellow and white curbs.
The only trekker coverage in Laos is of the monumental Patuxai arch, a large war memorial in Vientiane, with some footage taken from a tripod.
Savannakhet is a very flat city, with the only visible mountains located across the Mekong River in Thailand. The soil has a slight red tinge, though not as pronounced as in Pakse.
The southern city of Pakse is easily identified by its distinctive red soil and uniquely dry vegetation and nearby hills.
A 1380-meter long bridge that crosses the Mekong River next to Pakse is the only major bridge in Laos with Street View coverage.
